name: VITA shade guide

card.summary: The A1-D4 tooth-colour scale dentists use to describe and track whitening results.
card.note: A measuring scale, not a treatment; visual matching accuracy varies.

quick.overview:
The VITA shade guide is a set of tooth-coloured tabs used to name how light or dark teeth are, from A1 to D4.

It is a measurement reference, so it is used in studies and in forum talk to record whitening progress.
quick.mechanism: A clinician holds tabs next to the tooth and picks the closest match by value and chroma; instruments can also measure colour.
quick.risks: It carries no risk itself. Studies report coverage gaps in shade guides and differences between visual and instrument readings.

lead: The VITA classical shade guide is a set of tooth-coloured tabs, labelled A1 to D4, that dentists hold beside a patient's teeth to describe and match tooth colour. It is arranged by value (lightness) and chroma (colour intensity), with letter groups A (red-brown), B (red-yellow), C (grey) and D (red-grey) [1][19]. For anyone whitening their teeth to look better, it serves as a common yardstick for saying how light teeth are before and after treatment, so a change can be described as a number of shades gained [1][4].

In looksmaxxing and cosmetic dentistry, shade numbers are shorthand for how white teeth are, and results are quoted in shade steps. Wikipedia reports in-office bleaching commonly gives about 2 to 7 shades and at-home strips or trays about 1 or 2 [1]. The guide is made by VITA Zahnfabrik of Bad Säckingen, Germany, and has been on the market since 1956 [20][21].

Dental research has examined the guide itself, including its colour coverage, the accuracy of visual matching compared with instruments, and how it compares with instruments and newer guides such as the VITA 3D-Master [2][3][8][9][10][16][22]. Many whitening trials use it as the outcome scale, alongside spectrophotometer readings [4][7][12][13].

Whitening change is recorded as shade steps

angle.text: The guide does not whiten anything itself. It gives people a way to define their starting shade, set a target shade and check how much a whitening treatment has changed the look of their smile [1][4].

paras: The classical guide groups tabs by hue letter and a number for chroma. Practitioners in whitening and prosthodontics choose the tab that looks closest to a tooth under standard lighting and record its code [1]. VITA describes the classical A1-D4 as a 16-shade guide and an internationally recognised reference for tooth shade determination [21]. Dental technicians receive the selected shade when they make crowns, veneers or bridges, and a Japanese review of prosthodontic teamwork notes that shade selection with the guide is often subjective and can lead to miscommunication between dentist and laboratory [11].

Dentistry colour terms are used in a fixed order. A dental columnist writing in Dental Economics describes value as the most important factor in shade matching, followed by chroma and then hue, and argues that the classical guide's A-B-C-D arrangement by hue makes value matching harder [22].

Digital tools, including photography, intraoral scanners and spectrophotometers, supplement or replace visual choice. A 2024 study compared shade matching by an intraoral scanner, a spectrophotometer and visual assessment [8], and another measured the in-vivo repeatability of three intra-oral spectrophotometers [9].

VITA's company timeline dates the Lumin-VACUUM shade guide to 1956, the year the A-D grouping of tooth shades became known, and a 2008 Dental Economics article describes the classical system as introduced in Germany in 1956 by a denture technician and used as the standard for shade communication for more than fifty years [20][22]. The same timeline places the VITAPAN classical A1-D4 as 'the first uniform shade standard' alongside VITAPAN denture teeth in 1983, so sources differ on exactly which product carried which date [20].

VITA introduced the SYSTEM 3D-MASTER in 1998, which it describes as allowing tooth shades to be determined and reproduced systematically for the first time, based on research into how natural tooth shades are distributed in colour space [20][21]. The Dental Economics author describes it as having 26 natural shades plus three bleach shades, evenly distributed through colour space and notated by value, chroma and hue (for example, 3M1), and criticises the classical guide as arbitrary, with about two-thirds of tooth colour space under-represented [22]. The VITA Linearguide 3D-MASTER followed in 2008, and the classical guide, including a version with VITA Bleached Shades, was redesigned in 2021 [20]. The VITA Bleachedguide 3D-MASTER is listed as a visual solution for whitening, and VITA Easyshade V and LITE as digital shade-determination instruments [21].
A 1990 paper proposed a small-colour-difference equation linking shade-guide colours expressed in Munsell terms to CIE L*a*b* colour differences, the system used for dental tolerances [18].

Researchers frequently use the guide to measure bleaching results, for example by enrolling volunteers with teeth at shade A3 or darker and counting shade steps gained [4]. Newer trials commonly report both the classical guide and the VITA Bleachedguide, in shade guide units, alongside an instrument reading [12][13].

Wikipedia lists the expected shade gains of different products: in-office 2 to 7 shades, strips and gels about 1 to 2 shades within several days, trays 1 to 2 shades within about three days, toothpastes 1 to 2 with continued use, and rinses up to three months. It also reports that nearly half of an in-office change can rebound within a week, largely as teeth rehydrate [1].

In cosmetic-dentistry marketing and online whitening discussions, shade numbers function as a shared language: users quote their starting shade, a target and the steps gained, and dentists display before-and-after galleries labelled with the guide. Colour is also affected by cause: surface stains from tea, coffee, red wine or tobacco are usually removed by cleaning, intrinsic discoloration from fluorosis, tetracycline or trauma is generally treated with bleaching or restorations, and ageing darkens teeth as thin enamel lets dentin show through [19]. One survey cited on Wikipedia found the most common shade in a population fell between A1 and A3 [19].

A 1991 study examined the colour coverage of two shade guides, and a 1998 study compared a sphere spectrophotometer with human evaluation of tooth shade [2][3]. A 2025 paper titled 'How many tooth colors are there?' examines the range of natural tooth colour against fixed guides [10]. ClinicalTrials.gov lists small studies comparing visual, photographic and spectrophotometric matching, with 9 to 20 participants in the smaller ones and 210 patients in a 2026 study of how the order of shade presentation affects patient choice [5][6][15].

A 2014 randomised comparison examined selecting VITA classical shades using the VITA 3D-Master guide [16]. Perceived colour also depends on lighting, translucency and how the eye and brain interpret light [19].

Studies have evaluated the guide as a measurement tool. A 1991 study examined coverage errors of two shade guides, and a 1998 study compared a sphere spectrophotometer with human evaluation of tooth shade [2][3]. ClinicalTrials.gov lists small trials comparing visual, photographic and spectrophotometric shade matching [5][6]. Clinical bleaching trials use the guide as an outcome scale [4][7].

Examples include a 40-person trial of in-office light-activated systems in volunteers with shade A3 or darker [4], a 2005 comparison of over-the-counter, in-office and at-home bleaching to reach six grades of whitening [7], and an 80-person randomised trial comparing combined in-office plus at-home bleaching with at-home bleaching alone, which found slightly higher colour change in the first week for the combined group, no significant difference at the end, and more sensitivity with the combined approach [12]. A 40-person split-mouth trial of 40% hydrogen peroxide found no significant colour difference between gel mixed at the session and gel mixed a week earlier [13]. A 50-person trial examined violet LED with 35% carbamide peroxide [17].

The guide is a measuring tool, but its main use is to record the effect of whitening treatments, which have documented side effects. Wikipedia reports tooth sensitivity in 67 to 78 percent of people after in-office hydrogen peroxide treatment with heat, lasting about 4 to 39 days, chemical burns from poorly fitting trays, and unclear long-term effects of concentrations above 6 percent; whitening is contraindicated under age 16 and in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and the term 'bleachorexia' describes an unhealthy preoccupation with whitening [1].

Regulation differs by region. EU retail products are limited to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide, with up to 6 percent allowed under dental supervision for patients 18 or older; the US FDA endorses gels under 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or up to 16 percent carbamide peroxide; and in the UK the General Dental Council raised concerns in 2010 about untrained providers [1].

lore.intro: Shade numbers are widely quoted in teeth-whitening and cosmetic-dentistry discussion as a way of describing how white teeth are; the guide's own accuracy is debated mainly among dental researchers and clinicians [1][22].

claims.claim: Whitening can gain several shades on the guide in one visit
claims.believers: Practitioners and clinic marketing quote in-office gains of 2 to 7 shades in one visit [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports 2 to 7 shades in office and 1 to 2 for strips, trays and toothpastes, with nearly half of an in-office change rebounding within a week [1]; an 80-person trial found combined in-office plus at-home bleaching gave slightly more early colour change but no significant difference at the end [12].

claims.claim: The classical A1-D4 guide is the gold standard for judging tooth colour
claims.believers: It has been the shade-communication standard for more than fifty years and is VITA's internationally recognised reference [21][22].
claims.experts: A Dental Economics author describes it as arbitrary, with only about 14 tabs matching natural shades and about two-thirds of colour space under-represented, and research has compared it with instruments and with the 3D-Master [2][16][22].

claims.claim: A spectrophotometer or scanner is more reliable than the eye
claims.believers: Proponents of digital shade-taking say instruments remove subjectivity and the dentist-lab communication problems that visual matching causes [11].
claims.experts: A 2024 study compared an intraoral scanner, a spectrophotometer and visual assessment, and another measured the repeatability of three spectrophotometers; registered trials with 9 to 20 participants compared visual, photographic and instrument methods [8][9][5][6].

claims.believers: Many people pursue the lightest shades, including bleached shades beyond the classical range, and whitening ads quote shade gains [1][21].
claims.experts: Trials record shade change and sensitivity but a measuring scale does not tell which shade is preferred; a 210-patient study examined how presentation order affects patient shade selection, and 'bleachorexia' is used in the literature for an unhealthy preoccupation with whitening [1][15].

claims.claim: Over-the-counter strips and trays work about as well as in-office treatment
claims.believers: Home users report visible gains from strips, trays and whitening toothpastes [1].
claims.experts: A 2005 clinical study compared over-the-counter, in-office and at-home techniques for the time taken to reach six grades of whitening, with side effects and patient acceptance recorded; Wikipedia lists smaller typical gains for home products [7][1].
